title: In ‘Shux,’ Bicol band Kilyab calls out ‘ayuda’ politics, climate neglect
summary: Drawn from a Gen Z expression of disappointment, the track urges voters in Camarines Sur and across Bicol to look beyond band-aid relief efforts

blocks.text: GRASSROOTS MUSIC. Kilyab performs in the streets and at venues across Naga City and the Bicol region.
Drawn from a Gen Z expression of disappointment, the track urges voters in Camarines Sur and across Bicol to look beyond band-aid relief efforts

items: Bicol pop band Kilyab's new single 'Shux' addresses climate change and systemic neglect in their community, urging citizens to reflect on their voting choices.
The band highlights the exploitation of disasters by politicians for self-promotion and emphasizes the need for socially relevant music to inspire civic engagement.
Kilyab's lyrics criticize the disconnect between local leaders' priorities and community needs, linking environmental issues to political accountability and urging action against corruption.

ALBAY, Philippines – Bicol pop band Kilyab isn’t just singing about change — they’re marching for it in the streets, too. With their new single, “Shux,” the band pushes back against the idea that climate suffering is unavoidable, blaming decades of systemic neglect for the ongoing struggles in their community.

“Drawing inspiration from Camarines Sur, we saw how even delivering ayuda (relief aid) is being used to mind-condition voters instead of really solving the issues that worsen climate change,” songwriter and lead vocalist Karl Ramirez said.
“If we don’t talk and do something about it, most of our fellow citizens will continue to fall prey to the same system,” he added.

blocks.caption: PROTEST. Kilyab’s lead vocalist Karl Ramirez speaks on the importance of socially relevant songs during a rally against Pax Silica in Naga on November 17, 2026. Photo by Jascyl Jee Hugo Sayson

blocks.text: The band emphasized that voters are often left with almost no real alternatives when choosing their leaders, trapping them in a recurring cycle: enduring calamities while politicians exploit those same disasters for self-promotion.
“These politicians don’t even hide it anymore — they even post videos on their social media accounts showing them handing out money disguised as prizes during their relief operations,” Ramirez said.
For Ramirez, “Shux” reflects the band’s firm belief in using socially relevant music to awaken their fellow citizens — and help end the cycles of neglect in their province and the wider Bicol region.

“Now and any time is the right time to sing songs that reflect the hardship and condition of our nation, and inspire all of us to continue taking a stand against corruption and imperialism,” he noted.
Verna Velasco, Kilyab’s keyboardist and a Bicol Pop mentor who coined the song’s title, said the word comes from a Gen Z expression.
“Shux” is a shortened version of “shucks,” used to convey disdain or disappointment.
“Using the ‘shux’ expression feels like a call for the youth and their communities to be more vigilant, starting with reflecting on why we vote for the people we put into power,” Velasco said.

“Like what the lyrics ask, ‘Ba’t ba kasi sila ang binoto niyo?’ (Why did you vote for them in the first place?), the song explains to us that we also have a shared responsibility for the neglect happening now amid the sufferings and issues we face,” she added.

blocks.caption: CIVIC ADVOCACY. Bicol Pop band Kilyab performs its original hits in Naga City at major gatherings advocating for youth empowerment and anti-corruption accountability.

blocks.text: In a world quick to move past pressing issues, Velasco hopes the song will help people remember — especially when selecting new leaders.
That call for electoral reflection lands in a province long shaped by entrenched political power. Camarines Sur has been dominated by the Villafuerte dynasty for nearly 40 years.

In the 2025 midterm elections, the family maintained its grip on the province as Luis Raymund “LRay” Villafuerte reclaimed the gubernatorial seat, while his sons, Migz and Luigi, also secured seats in Congress. (READ: Iriga City bet decries harassment, vote buying in Camarines Sur).
Ramirez told Rappler that the song’s lyrics were written in one sitting during a songwriting class with Bicol Pop students back in April.
Set against soaring oil prices and looming warnings of a Super El Niño, the track was sparked by growing frustration over the government’s failure to step up.

“Our government can do major things regarding the climate crisis, or at least to ease the suffering of those affected. But instead of helping, we still allow some of our local watersheds — like Mount Isarog in Camarines Sur — to be destroyed,” Ramirez said.

That environmental vulnerability is already playing out on the ground. In 2025, San Jose Mayor Jerold Peña pointed out that rampant quarrying near the Rangas River had accelerated erosion within the Mount Isarog watershed and worsened flooding.

“What we are witnessing is not only the force of nature, but also the consequence of human actions — rampant quarrying and a widespread lack of understanding of the natural dynamics of the Rangas River,” Peña said at the time.

blocks.caption: SOCIAL RELEVANCE. Kilyab recorded its new single, ‘Shux,’ to reflect issues surrounding El Niño and inflation caused by bad governance.

blocks.text: A year later, in preparation for El Niño, the mayor assured residents that the local government had formed a task force to monitor the watershed and secure community water supplies, though he acknowledged that meeting agricultural demands during the dry season would remain a steep challenge.

For Kilyab, the strain on Mount Isarog and Bicol’s watersheds highlights a stark disconnect between what local leaders prioritize and what communities actually need to survive worsening climate impacts.

Rather than treating floods and dry spells as mere acts of nature, the band argues that years of unchecked quarrying, weak environmental enforcement, and band-aid relief operations are the real drivers of the region’s recurring crises — the exact cycle of neglect that “Shux” wants to expose.

Rooted in their environmental protection advocacy, Kilyab cuts straight to the heart of political accountability with the song’s biting line: “Bakit ba kasi sila ang binoto niyo? Oh ayan, naghihirap tayo (Why did you vote for them in the first place? Look now, we’re suffering).” – Rappler.com
